analysis.one_liner: Lets copyright holders get US internet providers to block foreign piracy websites.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026 with zero cosponsors and sits in the House Judiciary Committee with about three weeks left before the Congress ends in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a court process allowing copyright owners to seek orders blocking Americans' access to foreign websites accused of large-scale copyright infringement. U.S. internet providers, search engines, ad networks, and payment companies could be ordered to stop serving those sites. This is the same basic approach as the 2012 STOP Online Piracy Act (SOPA), which was shelved after a massive public outcry. As introduced, the bill has no cosponsors and has only been referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Large copyright holders — motion picture studios, music labels, book publishers, and other rights owners — gain a new legal tool to cut off foreign piracy sites at the U.S. level, rather than chasing them site by site in foreign courts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill establishes procedures for blocking access to foreign online locations engaged in copyright piracy, meaning copyright owners could get court orders directing U.S. internet service providers and related companies to stop serving designated foreign sites [S1].
For rights holders, this concentrates enforcement on the payment and traffic chokepoints inside the United States, which is cheaper and more effective than pursuing individual site operators abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users bear the risk that sites get blocked incorrectly, with no meaningful chance to contest; internet providers, search engines, ad networks, and payment companies bear compliance costs and legal risk for policing content they did not create.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet users, ISPs, search and ad platforms

drawbacks.text: Site-blocking orders can sweep in lawful websites, because a foreign site may host a mix of infringing and legal content, and defendants outside U.S. jurisdiction have limited ability to contest a block before it takes effect.

Routing blocking orders through U.S. internet infrastructure raises the same concerns that sank SOPA in 2012: interference with the internet's domain name system, burdens on smaller providers, and a censorship architecture that could be reused for purposes beyond piracy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Piracy is a real, ongoing loss for creators, and foreign-hosted infringing sites are genuinely hard to reach with existing law. But the mechanism this bill uses — blocking access at U.S. chokepoints based on court orders against sites no one in the U.S. controls — carries a real risk of overblocking lawful speech and imposes policing duties on companies that are not the infringers. Whether the enforcement gain outweighs the free-speech and compliance costs depends entirely on safeguards the bill text would need to show, and at this point the bill has no cosponsors or committee action to signal that those details have been worked out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2026, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and has sat there ever since with no cosponsors, no hearings, and no vote.

narrative.text: Darrell Issa (R-CA) introduced the bill in the House on September 14, 2026 [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S3].
No members have cosponsored it — the cosponsor count is zero [S2].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history after the referral [S3].
The 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027, leaving roughly three and a half months from introduction for the bill to clear committee and pass both chambers [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has gained anything concrete: the copyright industries are no worse off than before, and internet users face no new blocking regime. The status quo — piracy continues, and no site-blocking law exists — simply persists.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 14, 2026 and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party have signed on and no vote has occurred, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record yet [S2].

industries.industry: Motion picture, music, and publishing industries
industries.note: These rights holders would gain a powerful new tool to shut off U.S. traffic and payments to foreign piracy sites, something current law makes difficult. The gain comes at the cost of internet users' unfiltered access and raises overblocking risks, though the sites targeted are ones trafficking in infringing copies.

industries.industry: Internet service providers, search engines, ad networks, and payment processors
industries.note: These companies would be ordered to block or stop serving designated foreign sites, taking on compliance costs and legal risk for policing third-party content. Their burden tracks users' own interest in avoiding an infrastructure of site blocking.

industries.industry: Foreign-owned pirate websites and their operators
industries.note: Sites generating revenue from infringing film, music, and software would lose access to U.S. visitors and payment channels — the direct target of the bill, whose removal most users would not miss.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee hearing scheduled, and the Congress ending January 3, 2027, this bill is almost certain to die without a vote. A sponsor pursuing site-blocking seriously would typically need to refile with a broad coalition and committee support in the next Congress — and even then, this approach has faced organized public opposition before.
